Google’s Gemini 3.8 Flash is built for agents, while its Cyber twin hunts vulnerabilities

📅 03 Sep 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2173 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Venturebeat

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Google keeps cranking out Flash models: the manufacturer on Wednesday declared two versions of a newly introduced 3.8 Flash.
  • Google keeps cranking out Flash models: the tech giant on Wednesday announced two versions of a upcoming 3.8 Flash.
  • The variants include a standard Flash, a “workhorse” model for agentic tasks, software development, and multi-step reasoning, and Flash Cyber optimized for vulnerability detection and mitigation.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Google keeps cranking out Flash models: the manufacturer on Wednesday declared two versions of a newly introduced 3.8 Flash. The variants include a standard Flash, a “workhorse” model for agentic tasks, software development, and multi-step reasoning, and Flash Cyber optimized for vulnerability detection and mitigation.Google CEO Sundar Pichai mentioned in an X post that 3.8 Flash delivers “significant leaps” from 3.7 Flash across software engineering, agentic tasks, and multi-step reasoning. For instance, it outperformed many large frontier models on the DeepSWE coding benchmark, at far lower cost. Meanwhile, Flash Cyber is the company’s “most capable” cybersecurity model, Pichai said; it also matches frontier-level performance when it comes to discovering vulnerabilities and patching them at scale. The model achieved 86.2% on the CyberGym cybersecurity benchmark and 47.2% on CWE-Bench, which evaluates AI patching abilities. In an internal Google benchmark, the model achieved a more than 70% success rate discovering vulnerabilities across 20 programming languages, Pichai said. 3.8 is Google’s third Flash release in six weeks and comes rapidly on the heels of version 3.7. 3.8 working "harder" with "greater diligence"3.8 Flash is available now in Gemini Enterprise; devs can try it out in the Gemini API via Google AI Studio, Google Antigravity, Android Studio, or generate UIs in Stitch. It is priced at $0.75 per million input tokens and $3.75 per million output tokens — the same introductory pricing as Gemini 3.7 Flash — and users can customize and adjust model effort levels based on their needs around quality, cost, and latency. For instance, when compute efficiency is a priority, they can adjust to lower token overhead, or simply continue working with 3.7 Flash, which is “fully supported for efficiency-first workloads,” Google senior product director Tulsee Doshi and Gemini security lead Raluca Ada Popa wrote in a blog post. “3.8 Flash works harder,” exhibiting “greater diligence” with complex tasks like executing extra reasoning steps, although at times it may use more tokens to maximize performance, Doshi and Popa note. The model has a 1M-token input window and a 64K-token output limit, and can ingest text as well as images, audio, video, and PDF files. 3.8 Flash was evaluated across numerous benchmarks testing coding, multimodal capabilities, computer use, long-context and knowledge work, and scientific reasoning. Google says it also does well in specialized knowledge domains requiring more in-depth analysis and reporting. For instance, the model outperformed its predecessor and other frontier models on benchmarks like Vals Finance Agent V2 for finance, and Harvey's Legal Agent Benchmark for law; it also scored 54.9% on Humanity’s Last Exam (HLE)-Verified, reflecting its ability to take on multi-step reasoning tasks across subjects like math, science, and humanities. In one example shared by Google, Gemini 3.8 Flash built a game with a simple prompt using looping techniques in Google’s Antigravity platform. The game uses puzzles, storytelling that changes based on the environment, and images and textures from Nano Banana to create a 3D experience (in this case a wizard navigating a castle). In other instances, the model created a fully-functional DOS version of Google Maps featuring interactive locations, directions, and street views; a 3D visualizer that automatically decomposed devices into layers for inspection with a slider capability; and a topographic map of famous geographical sites based on real datasets from the U.S. Geological Survey, complete with real-time cross-sections, 2D projections, and scientific explanations. According to Arena.ai, 3.8 Flash landed at No. 14 in Agent Arena, ranking above DeepSeek-V4-Pro, and showed a significant jump over Gemini 3.7 Flash (which sits all the way down at No. 32). It debuted at No. 7 in Text Arena, ahead of Claude Opus 5 and Gemini 3.7 Flash. It improved over 3.7 Flash in several areas: multi-turn requests, writing, literature, and language, longer queries, hard prompts, coding, instruction following, software and IT services, and business, management and financial ops. Flash Cyber is already securing Google's codeFlash Cyber is initially being rolled out to “trusted defenders” through Google’s Fairwind Program, which prioritizes government authorities, critical-infrastructure operators, and other partners looking for advanced cyber defense capabilities. Organizations can apply for access. Google says the model version has undergone “rigorous training” in the cybersecurity domain and represents a “significant leap in prompt injection robustness.” It is particularly adept at autonomous vulnerability discovery — at least, based on internal Gemini benchmarks — and automated patching. It is also very good at coding, Popa said in a video. The goal was to equip defenders with expert-level capabilities to give them a leg up over threat actors (whether malicious, fellow AI agents, or human hackers). “We have invested in vulnerability fixing from the start, and prioritized it over offensive capabilities like exploitation,” Doshi and Popa explain. The model ships a more permissive set of mitigations for cybersecurity safeguards — which is why, for now, it is only being shared with limited partners — and safeguards against misuse in cyber offense and areas like chemical, biological, radiological, and nuclear (CBRN).Google is already using 3.8 Flash Cyber to secure its own code; it produced 2.6 times more correct patches in Chrome vulnerabilities versus much larger commercial models. Wiz — which Google acquired earlier this year at a historic $32 billion — reported that 3.8 Flash Cyber had 7.5% to 9.7% higher recall of real-world vulnerabilities on an internal penetration testing benchmark at 2.3 to 5.2 times lower cost than leading frontier models. Similarly, Google’s Cloud Vulnerability Research found a critical foundational vulnerability in less than 2 hours with 3.8 Flash Cyber. Typically, that research and discovery would take months, Google claims. AI agents are “incredibly skilled” at finding and exploiting vulnerabilities, Popa said. Scanning large codebases with big AI models is expensive, and defenders are overwhelmed. “In cybersecurity, attackers need only find one significant flaw over millions of lines of code. Defenders have to remove every one of those flaws to be able to defend against attackers.” Doug Turner, engineering director for Chrome, described a “vulnerability apocalypse” in recent months due to generative AI. “Simply overnight, we saw a hockey stick increase in the number of software vulnerabilities reported through our vulnerability research program,” he said in a video. One interesting vulnerability 3.8 Flash Cyber discovered had been in Chromium and Chrome for 13 years, he explained. It was a “very subtle bug” that dozens, if not hundreds, of engineers looked at but never flagged. “Gemini 3.8 Flash Cyber is going to allow us to create better suggested fixes so that developers’ lives can get a lot easier.”.

Some even require players to complete specific challenges.

There are two types of GTA players: those who play the game as intended, and those who instantly try to create as much chaos as possible. Those latter folks are typically helped along by the franchise's many iconic cheat codes. We have good news and bad news for these players. Cheat codes are still a thing in GTA 6, but the process to unlock them is more convoluted than ever before.

Players must complete all of the main story missions to start unlocking cheat codes. PC Gamer claims that all 91 story missions must be bested before cheat codes enter the picture, and that's just the beginning.

Beating the game lets people enter a number of useful cheat codes, including one that provides a $250,000 cash drop and another that gives unlimited focus (the game's time-slowing mechanic.) You just need the actual codes, many of which are listed here.

All GTA 6 Cheats—Best Grand Theft Auto 6 Cheat Codeshttps://t.co/JWOCocGBN2.

— Tom Henderson (@_Tom_Henderson_) November 18, 2026.

According to recent reports, other codes, however, are gated behind specific tasks outside the main story. For instance, you'll need to lose a three-star wanted level 25 times to unlock a code that automatically raises your wanted level. Want an instant influx of ammo? Win 25 bronze (or higher) medals at various shooting ranges.

This is a bit frustrating to those who treat GTA less like a video game and more like a destruction sandbox, and stands in stark contrast to how Rockstar did things with GTA 5. Cheat codes were available right from the jump, though they did momentarily turn off achievements.

According to recent reports, GTA 6 looks to be eliminating some of the arcade-like aspects of previous titles in favor of realistic immersion, which many people saw coming after the success of Red Dead Redemption 2. Players in the fictional world of Leonida have to keep fuel tanks full, which is new, and there's a limit on how many weapons can be carried at once.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, on a walk through Vice City, you might pass tourists taking vacation photos, someone playing Frisbee with their dog, or a bouncer working the door at a club. A little farther down the street, you could see a carjacking, a police chase, or someone dancing on the roof of a car. And all of that can happen while you're just on your way to buy a T-shirt or pair of shoes.

Ahead of Grand Theft Auto VI’s Nov. 19 release on PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X/S, early reviews, gameplay clips, and livestreamers are giving us a better sense of who we'll meet in Vice City and across Leonida, Rockstar's fictional version of Florida. The game is packed full of NPCs, short for non-player characters, and stopping to talk to one can lead to anything from a quick hello to a whole new side quest.

The detail that went into many of these characters is clearly impressive, or as one X user mentioned, "nothing short of magic," which makes sense considering Rockstar put together an entire team in Los Angeles to give the people you pass on the street more personality. The studio created roughly 600,000 animations for its NPCs, Edge reported last month.

Industry observers note that players are already posting their strangest NPC encounters, and we're learning a lot about how they work. Now of course, a short video can be hard to authenticate, especially when AI can mimic gameplay footage, so note that we haven't independently verified every clip making the rounds. Nevertheless, here's what early reviews and gameplay clips suggest can happen when you run into some of these characters.

According to recent reports, in GTA 6, you can greet or taunt NPCs as you pass, and they will all react in different ways depending in part on their individual temperament, what they've seen, and how you've treated them, according to Edge. Some are especially hostile and can pick a fight, slap you, and even follow you onto the road. In a gameplay clip posted by the GTA 6 Updates account, another driver chases Jason after he cuts her off. One streamer Paisley found NPCs in will "hunt you down and try to murder you if you hit their car.".

Recent findings suggest that "Even the grandmas in Vice City are dangerous," according to one X user, who shared a clip of an elderly woman in a scooter robbing another NPC at gunpoint. When the player intervened, she turned her weapon on them. "GTA 6 NPCs are absolutely unhinged," the user added.

NPCs are often causing chaos in the background. In one clip, a man was filling up his gas tank when he lit himself on fire. Another saunters the beach with a pet alligator on a leash. One NPC "asked Jason for a cigarette, spat it into the air, caught it in his mouth, and then high-fived himself when Jason left him hanging".

Sources indicate that there is a wide mix of people in the game, and their jobs vary by district. Rockstar built nearly 500 repeatable scenes across 12,500 locations. Even overheard dialogue can be worth sharing — in a clip from streamer N3ON's playthrough, he is speechless after hearing an NPC say "clip that." Not even Leonida is safe from the latest streamer lingo. The best tech deal this week The Apple iPhone 18 Pro is free right now with T-Mobile Products available for purchase through affiliate links. The Apple iPhone 18 Pro is free right now with T-Mobile.

An NPC's job shapes the options you get when approaching them. For example, Rockstar's extended gameplay footage shows Jason choosing how to get a bouncer's attention. Shopkeepers can also jump into action when trouble walks through the door. In The Verge's review, gang members followed the reviewer into a clothing store. The shopkeeper called the police, forcing the reviewer to empty the register before making a getaway. And that's just one example — we've seen other clips of NPCs calling the cops on Jason throughout the game.

Recent findings suggest that you can also come across police who are busy with someone else. During one demo, Jason passed two officers who were already making an arrest. Streamer BlueThunderReal described getting close enough to a police perimeter that officers told them to "clear out.".

According to recent reports, some of the people working across Leonida are also part of Jason and Lucia's story. In the Keys, Jason works for smuggler Brian Heder and knows one of his associates, Cal Hampton. On the music side, nightclub owner Boobie Ike runs a record label with Dre'Quan Priest, and the rap duo Real Dimez are signed to it. Then there's Raul Bautista, a bank robber who’s always looking for people to bring in on a job.

In a recent development, rockstar worked out some of those connections far beyond the named cast. Senior design director Steve Messinger mentioned that the team mapped how drugs move through gang compounds and reach buyers on the street, even though players might only see a small part of that operation.

Sources indicate that other people come into the story because you decide to stop. Rockstar told Destructoid it built more than 1,000 encounters whose timing can depend on how much attention you give them. Drive past and you might hear the first line of dialogue and get another chance to stop later. Stick around and you might finish the encounter then and there, or meet someone who has more to say the next time you cross paths.

Side missions can also grow out of relationships Jason already has. His old Army friend Bret Vogel, for instance, teaches him how to track deer and gives him more animals to hunt, as Mashable reported.

And sometimes the person you help has a pretty specific plan for what comes next. In Jason Schreier's Bloomberg review, Jason stops to help someone who was hit by a corporate delivery driver. The person decides to sue the company and offers Jason a cut if he'll serve as a witness.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Defense mogul Palmer Luckey — whose $90 billion drone and weapons startup Anduril is flush with government contracts — is still the kind of guy who prepares for the worst.

During Luckey’s conversation with Andrew Ross Sorkin at The Newly introduced York Times’ DealBook Summit on Wednesday, the billionaire implied that Americans should batten down the hatches in case there are rough times ahead. Luckey himself has taken steps to prepare for a potential cataclysmic event, he said.

According to recent reports, the conversation took place against the backdrop of a series of recent large-scale outages — at Apple, at Microsoft, at the NSA, and at the Federal Aviation Administration — that have led to concerns that America may be under attack by cyberthreat actors. The government has noted that this is not the case, but Luckey cryptically teased that there may be more to the story.

In a recent development, “Look, all the 4chan schizo posters are like 12 hours ahead of the mainstream media on this. You guys are going to find out what’s going on soon enough,” he noted.

Sorkin also asked Luckey to expound on comments made backstage “about what might be a cyber war that seems to be going on around us.”.

Luckey described a “mismatch” between the sophisticated AI-powered cyberattacks that exist today and “old, outdated systems that are not able to adopt technology as rapidly as it is developed.” He added: “I think people are going to have to pick up the pace. It’s time to start running.”.

Recent findings suggest that “What does that mean? Are you a prepper?” Sorkin asked.

Industry observers note that luckey didn’t deny the characterization. “I own a missile base 200 feet underground,” he answered, to audience laughter. “It’s a funny joke, but a missile base is actually a pretty bad way to run from the apocalypse. Everyone knows exactly where you are, and they [bases] are designed to take a hit from a nuclear weapon, a blast overpressure event.”.

It has been revealed that however, he had some qualifications on the prepper label. “The point is, like everyone should have three days of water. Everyone should have three days of dry food. If you have prescription medication, don’t go refill it when you run out. Make sure you refill it 72 hours before you run out.”.

“People used to be taught this in middle school, and now everyone who remembers that is treated like a nut,” he added.

Industry observers note that it should be pointed out that preparing for the apocalypse is not necessarily a latest interest for Luckey. In 2017, a person familiar with the billionaire described him as a “prepper” and the bunker that was broached Wednesday is one of several decommissioned Cold War era underground bases that Luckey has purchased over the years. In 2024, he revealed that his massive video game collection is housed in one of them.

#1147. Microsoft AI’s MAI-Transcribe-2 undercuts OpenAI, Google and ElevenLabs on price and speed

📅 03 Sep 2026 • ⏱️ 24m • 📚 Deep Dive (4731 w)
📖 Baca

Microsoft AI’s MAI-Transcribe-2 undercuts OpenAI, Google and ElevenLabs on price and speed

📅 03 Sep 2026 | ⏱️ 24 min read (4731 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Venturebeat

⏱️ ~24 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that microsoft AI on Thursday released MAI-Transcribe-2, a speech-recognition model the tech giant claims is faster, more accurate, and cheaper than anything OpenAI, Google, or ElevenLabs currently sells.
  • In a recent development, microsoft AI on Thursday released MAI-Transcribe-2, a speech-recognition model the organization indicates is faster, more accurate, and cheaper than anything OpenAI, Google, or ElevenLabs currently sells.
  • Industry observers note that that figure deserves a pause.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that microsoft AI on Thursday released MAI-Transcribe-2, a speech-recognition model the tech giant claims is faster, more accurate, and cheaper than anything OpenAI, Google, or ElevenLabs currently sells. Then it priced the thing at 10 cents per hour of audio.That figure deserves a pause. When Microsoft AI shipped the first model in this line just five months ago, it charged $0.36 an hour. Thursday's early-bird price cuts that by roughly 72%. For an enterprise processing 100,000 hours of call-center audio a year — a modest volume for a large bank or telecom — the bill drops from $36,000 to $10,000. At that level, transcription stops being a line item anyone argues about.The release arrives as Microsoft executes a strategy that would have seemed implausible two years ago: building its own frontier-class models one modality at a time, then steadily swapping them into products that once ran on OpenAI's technology. Transcription is the modality where that plan has moved fastest, and MAI-Transcribe-2 is its clearest proof point yet. It also offers a preview of how the world's most valuable software company intends to compete in AI without depending on the partner it spent $13 billion to cultivate.What MAI-Transcribe-2 does and why the feature list matters to enterprise buyersThe model transcribes audio in 60 languages, up from 43 in June's MAI-Transcribe-1.5 and 25 in April's original release. It runs on Microsoft Foundry, the company's model marketplace for developers, and in MAI Playground, its testing environment. Microsoft says it built the model for the messy audio that real businesses generate — background noise, low-quality recordings, overlapping speech — rather than clean studio conditions.More important than the language count is what Microsoft has bundled into the base product. Speaker diarization sorts out who remarked what in a multi-person recording, which is the difference between a wall of text and a usable meeting transcript. Word-level timestamps attach a precise time marker to every word, enabling search, editing, and alignment with video. Keyword biasing lets developers feed the model a list of drug names, product codes, or employee names so it stops mangling domain jargon. Automatic language identification means customers no longer have to declare the language in advance.Two features stand out for their specificity. A configurable output style offers a "verbatim" mode that preserves every "um," false start, and stutter for compliance and legal teams, alongside a "clean" mode that strips fillers for readable captions and notes. And code switching handles conversations that drift between languages mid-sentence; Microsoft explicitly names Hinglish and Spanglish, a nod to the Indian and U.S. Hispanic markets where a single customer-service call might toggle languages a dozen times. Specialty vendors have historically charged premiums for each of these capabilities. Microsoft is including all of them for a dime.How to read Microsoft's FLEURS and Artificial Analysis benchmark claimsMicrosoft makes three performance claims, each resting on a different measuring stick, and technical buyers should understand what each one captures and what it misses.The first is that MAI-Transcribe-2 ranks number one on FLEURS across 60 languages with an average word error rate of 5.2%. FLEURS is a benchmark Google researchers published in 2022, built from native speakers reading roughly 2,000 sentences in each of 102 languages — about 12 hours of speech per language. It is the standard yardstick for multilingual speech recognition because it lets you compare a model's Swahili against its Swedish on identical content. Word error rate, its metric, simply counts substitutions, insertions, and deletions against a human reference; 5.2% means roughly one word in 20 is wrong. But FLEURS is read speech, not conversation, and Microsoft's average has actually risen from the 3.7% it reported for MAI-Transcribe-1.5 in June. That almost certainly reflects broader coverage rather than regression — averaging across 60 languages instead of 43 means folding in low-resource languages where every model struggles — but buyers should request the per-language breakdown.The second claim is that the model ranks second on the Artificial Analysis word-error-rate leaderboard and defines that firm's accuracy-latency Pareto frontier. Artificial Analysis is an independent benchmarker that tests models through their public APIs, measuring what a customer actually gets. Its index blends simulated agent conversations, European Parliament speeches, and corporate earnings calls, weighting heavily toward English business speech. It runs on Microsoft Foundry, the company's model marketplace for developers, and in MAI Playground, its testing environment. Microsoft says it built the model for the messy audio that real businesses generate — background noise, low-quality recordings, overlapping speech — rather than clean studio conditions.

Speaker diarization sorts out who noted what in a multi-person recording, which is the difference between a wall of text and a usable meeting transcript. Word-level timestamps attach a precise time marker to every word, enabling search, editing, and alignment with video. Keyword biasing lets developers feed the model a list of drug names, product codes, or employee names so it stops mangling domain jargon. Automatic language identification means owners no longer have to declare the language in advance.

A configurable output style offers a "verbatim" mode that preserves every "um," false start, and stutter for compliance and legal teams, alongside a "clean" mode that strips fillers for readable captions and notes. #1146. Trump abandons his FDA nominee, and Senate scraps vote on his NSF pick

Trump abandons his FDA nominee, and Senate scraps vote on his NSF pick

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (665 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ars Technica

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In the span of less than 24 hours, two Trump administration nominees have suffered sudden blows—Trump’s pick to lead the Food and Drug Administration and his pick to lead the National Science Foundation.
  • Late Tuesday evening, Axios reported that the White House had abruptly withdrawn its controversial nomination of Heidi Overton to lead the FDA.
  • In her confirmation hearing in September, Overton consistently stonewalled senators on every topic, refusing to directly answer even softball questions from friendly Republicans, leaving lawmakers on both sides of the aisle openly frustrated.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In the span of less than 24 hours, two Trump administration nominees have suffered sudden blows—Trump’s pick to lead the Food and Drug Administration and his pick to lead the National Science Foundation.

Late Tuesday evening, Axios reported that the White House had abruptly withdrawn its controversial nomination of Heidi Overton to lead the FDA. Overton, a top conservative domestic policy aide in the White House, has drawn criticism and skepticism from Republicans and Democrats alike over her stances on vaccines, abortion, vapes, and birth control. Overton opposes abortion—though perhaps not strongly enough for some Republicans—and supported Trump and Kennedy’s decried anti-vaccine policies and statements, vexing Democrats.

In her confirmation hearing in September, Overton consistently stonewalled senators on every topic, refusing to directly answer even softball questions from friendly Republicans, leaving lawmakers on both sides of the aisle openly frustrated. The questions she dodged included those on how she would handle the FDA’s current safety review of the abortion pill, mifepristone, which extensive data has established is extremely safe. She also wouldn’t say whether she agreed with Trump when he falsely claimed the measles vaccine is “quite lethal” or that children are given vaccine doses the “size of a soda bottle.” Overton repeatedly refused to answer whether Trump could ever be wrong.

Axios quoted a senior Trump administration official as saying that Overton’s nomination was dropped because she “lacks the support on the Hill to move forward with her confirmation.”.

It has been revealed that the Senate’s Health, Education, Labor and Pensions (HELP) Committee, chaired by Bill Cassidy (R-La.), was scheduled to vote on Overton’s nomination Wednesday. In a social media post Tuesday night, after her nomination was withdrawn, Cassidy said he believed she had a “viable confirmation path.” But he said the nomination was “abandoned” after some anti-abortion senators sought commitments from her that they couldn’t get. “The Administration withdrew Dr. Overton rather than make such commitments,” Cassidy said.

“Unfortunately, with the limited time left, confirming a permanent FDA Commissioner will fall to Senate Democrats,” Cassidy noted.

After Overton’s last-minute withdrawal, the HELP committee’s agenda for Wednesday was updated again this morning to scrap a scheduled vote on Jim O’Neill, who was Trump’s nominee to run the NSF.

Recent findings suggest that O’Neill has been criticized for lacking the science experience needed to run the foundation. In the past, O’Neill worked as a Silicon Valley investor and entrepreneur and became a close ally of Peter Thiel. But under Trump, O’Neill has been the deputy secretary of the Department of Health and Human Services and served as acting director of the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. O’Neill took over the latter role after the former director, Susan Monarez, was ousted from it less than a month after her Senate confirmation. She later told Senators Kennedy fired her for refusing to blindly approve vaccine recommendations from his anti-vaccine advisors.

In remarks this morning, Cassidy said that O’Neill “did not do enough to stand up for science and against irresponsible decisions and statements from [Health] Secretary [Robert F.] Kennedy [Jr.].” As an example, Cassidy specifically referenced O’Neill’s role in the firing of Monarez. “Several members of the [HELP] committee had concerns regarding this,” Cassidy said.

“This time requires leadership and fortitude and standing up for what is right,” Cassidy added.

Industry observers note that the NSF has been hard hit by the Trump administration and actions by Elon Musk’s DOGE. The NSF has been forced to cancel hundreds of research grants and taken brutal cuts to its budget and staff in the past two years. In April, the Trump administration also terminated all members of the board that steers the NSF, called the National Science Board. Former members feared that it would make way for O’Neill to stack the board with political allies, pointing to how Trump filled the President’s Council of Advisors on Science and Technology with tech billionaires—including leaders of Meta, Google, Oracle, and Nvidia—instead of top scientists and researchers.

#1145. You can finally edit an Instagram Story without deleting it

You can finally edit an Instagram Story without deleting it

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (369 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Engadget

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • There’s a 15-minute window to fix typos and make other changes.
  • Meta is finally addressing a particularly annoying quirk I'm confident has affected just about all of Instagram's 3 billion users at one point or another.
  • Write a different caption altogether?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

There’s a 15-minute window to fix typos and make other changes.

Meta is finally addressing a particularly annoying quirk I'm confident has affected just about all of Instagram's 3 billion users at one point or another. More than a decade after Stories became a central part of the photo-sharing app, the company is giving users the ability to edit their posts after they've been shared.

Want to fix an embarrassing typo? Add or change the music? Write a different caption altogether? All that is now possible without the need to delete a post, Instagram head Adam Mosseri shared. With the change, Instagram users have a 15-minute window to tweak their Stories while preserving views, likes and replies.

In a recent development, deleting and re-uploading a Story might not seem like a huge inconvenience, but it can be frustrating when it happens within a sequence of posts. Since Stories slides appear reverse chronologically, there's no way to delete and re-share a post and have it appear in the same place if there are other images immediately before and after. It's even worse if you're a professional creator or social media manager and need to worry about a do-over affecting your metrics. So while the 15-minute editing window only gives a little additional flexibility, it does give you the chance to catch errors that have already been posted.

Industry observers note that it's not clear why such a seemingly obvious change took so long for Instagram to implement. Meta has long allowed customers to edit regular Instagram posts after the fact. "A lot of people have been asking for this, so I'm excited to get this one out there," Mosseri wrote.

According to recent reports, the feature is rolling out now. Once editing is available, you'll be able to tweak Stories from the "more" menu and selecting "edit story." Posts that have been edited will include an "edited" label when others view them.

According to recent reports, instagram is also tweaking a few aspects of the Stories composer too. The app is updating its available background color options to include gradients and other effects. It's also making it easier to share and format several images at once.

It has been revealed that next year’s fall iPhone lineup is expected to include 20th anniversary redesigned Pro models and an iPhone Duo 2. Here’s what to expect per the latest leaks.

Rumors for next year’s flagship latest iPhone models are ramping up. Earlier today, we got a release timing update on iPhone 18 and iPhone Air 2 and learned that Apple may have multiple iPhone 20 Pro designs in testing.

Now more details have arrived via Weibo leakers Digital Chat Station and Fixed Focus Digital, who focus on the highly-anticipated fresh iPhone Pro models and also the iPhone Duo 2.

Recent findings suggest that fixed Focus Digital indicates the ‘iPhone 20 Pro’ will indeed return to a curved design, similar to the iPhone Air with more rounded edges. This echoes what the leaker shared earlier this week, but there’s one fresh tidbit: he says early prototypes include a titanium frame.

Sources indicate that apple used titanium for the iPhone 15 Pro and 16 Pro, then abandoned it with the 17 Pro and 18 Pro. Titanium is used on the iPhone Air though. With next year’s 20th anniversary Pro models taking design cues from the Air, it sounds like titanium could return.

Leaker Digital Chat Station, in a reply to this post about iPhone Duo 2, adds that the 20 Pro series will be larger in size and have a bezel-free, quad-curved display.

Regarding the Duo 2, he says it will have the same 7.6-inch inner display and 5.4-inch outer display as the first model. The side button with integrated Touch ID remains unchanged as well.

On the possibility of Face ID being added, he claims it’s “questionable.” He suggests internal components might require too many changes, but doesn’t offer inside information.

Industry observers note that which fresh model are you more interested in: the iPhone 20 Pro or iPhone Duo 2? Let us know in the comments.

Nvidia’s rise, visualized

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Whatever doesn’t rock the mind-bogglingly profitable boat.
  • Recent findings suggest that what’s next for Nvidia?
  • In a recent development, if someone handed you $8,300 every second, what would you do?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

What’s next for Nvidia? Whatever doesn’t rock the mind-bogglingly profitable boat.

Recent findings suggest that what’s next for Nvidia? Whatever doesn’t rock the mind-bogglingly profitable boat.

In a recent development, if someone handed you $8,300 every second, what would you do? That’s how much pure profit Nvidia now makes. By the time you finish reading this paragraph, Nvidia will likely have cleared $45,000 and change.

Industry observers note that it’s easy to look at Nvidia, a company that just lost its visionary founder CEO due to a series of scandals, and think that the company and maybe the entire AI industry are in terrible trouble. Perhaps so?

But I want you to understand: Nvidia isn’t your average semi-successful manufacturer that might tempt a latest CEO to fix things that are broken. It is a company so staggeringly, mind-bogglingly successful it’ll do everything in its power not to rock the boat. There is so much money at stake.

It’s so much money that when I heard about Jensen Huang’s resignation, my first thought was: I need a way to visualize this jaw-dropping amount of money for you. I want to show you that Nvidia has risen so far, so fast, that rival chipmakers AMD, Intel, and Qualcomm barely qualify as competition now.

Sources indicate that if you’re on a desktop OS, you could mouse over each dot in our chart above to see the staggering sums. But we built another way to visualize the rise of Nvidia I like even better. It’s a horizontal bar graph that not only puts Nvidia’s revenue growth in perspective, but highlights you its monster profits right alongside them — plus the world events that made Nvidia a star.

TL;DR: The crypto boom and the great GPU shortage have nothing on the AI boom. Those earlier periods saw Nvidia’s profits briefly peak at $1.24 billion and $3 billion a quarter respectively, while the rise of data centers has driven them to $65 billion per quarter with no sign of stopping.

Yes, Jensen may have set a trillion dollars of Nvidia’s market cap on fire — from around $5 trillion at the start of November to “only” $3.6 trillion now — but the smoldering company is raking in $700 million in profit a day on average.

Put another way: Nvidia could give a $1 million bonus to every one of its 42,000 employees, every three months, without running out of cash. Or, you know, Nvidia could end world hunger or provide clean water for everyone, now that it’s making over $200 billion in pure profit a year.

Maybe that’d make people feel differently about data centers?

Recent findings suggest that but even if we stick to self-serving capitalism, you’re probably still a happy investor if you bought Nvidia a decade ago. A $1,000 investment 10 years ago is now worth over $67,000. You’d have over $1 million if you invested $15,000 back then.

According to recent reports, and make no mistake, Nvidia is sticking to capitalism. Nvidia interim CEO Colette Kress just promised to return as much money to investors as possible on the firm’s November 17th earnings call. “Going forward, we intend to return all excess free cash flow net of strategic uses to shareholders,” she declared. “All” is a lot more than the 50 percent baseline that Jensen promised five months ago.

Nvidia isn’t the only manufacturer whose fortunes have risen this dramatically. RAMageddon revealed that just three companies — Samsung, SK Hynix, and Micron — controlled nearly 90 percent of the entire global DRAM market, and those three have repeatedly signaled that they’d prefer to celebrate record profits instead of ramping up production too fast.

But while their revenues and profits have been skyrocketing even faster over the past year or so, even Big RAM hasn’t caught the AI wave quite the same way as Nvidia. Samsung, of course, doesn’t just make memory — its revenue numbers include phones, tablets, TVs, home appliances, chips, displays, camera sensors, audio, networking equipment, medical equipment, and more.

In the most recent quarter, Micron made $37.7 billion in profit, SK Hynix made $29.8 billion, and Samsung came in at around $55.3 billion, but they’re all shy of Nvidia’s $65.3 billion. Historically, RAM has also been a bit more cyclical: Both Micron and SK Hynix actually lost money in 2023 because they produced too much memory.

On its latest earnings call, the first since cofounder Jensen Huang’s resignation, interim CEO and CFO Colette Kress reinforced the idea that Nvidia expects the good times to keep on rolling.

According to recent reports, asked how things might change under newly introduced management, she suggested that they wouldn’t: “From a business perspective, it’s business as usual,” she noted. She added that the company has secured the backing of customers and suppliers including TSMC, the all-notable firm that actually fabricates Nvidia’s chips.

It has been revealed that “Our momentum is real, our demand is accelerating, our supply is growing. Our customers and partners are with us, and employees are committed,” she claimed. “We’ve got this.”.

Industry observers note that nvidia claims it’ll rake in even more money next quarter, with projected revenue of $130 billion. Profit may be proportionally smaller since gross margins are estimated to drop to 71–72 percent (compared to nearly 75 percent), but Kress mentioned Nvidia intends to get them up as high as 73 percent next year.

Sources indicate that in other words: This astounding gravy train isn’t going anywhere. At least that’s the strategy.

Stevie Bonifield contributed to this story.

#1142. America’s AI Chip War Is Heating Up in the Dumbest Possible Ways

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1299 w)

America’s AI Chip War Is Heating Up in the Dumbest Possible Ways

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1299 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: WIRED

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that this week, the Trump administration made it significantly harder for Chinese companies to access some of the world’s most advanced AI chips.
  • Sources indicate that but under newly introduced plans confirmed on Monday, overseas data centers that want to provide large amounts of computing power to China will have to get special licenses and deal with other annoying new kinds of red tape.
  • These are not latest policy ideas, and similar proposals have been kicking around in Washington for a while.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that this week, the Trump administration made it significantly harder for Chinese companies to access some of the world’s most advanced AI chips. For years, tech firms like Alibaba and ByteDance could rent computing power from data centers overseas, allowing them to use powerful Nvidia chips they were generally prohibited from physically importing into China. This is known as remote access.

Sources indicate that but under newly introduced plans confirmed on Monday, overseas data centers that want to provide large amounts of computing power to China will have to get special licenses and deal with other annoying new kinds of red tape. The White House also imposed stricter rules on shipments of advanced chips to five countries, including Singapore and Malaysia, where US officials suspect significant levels of smuggling may have taken place.

These are not latest policy ideas, and similar proposals have been kicking around in Washington for a while. But the timing of Monday’s announcement is impossible to ignore. Yes, this is about Jensen Huang’s sex life.

As you’ve probably heard by now, the Nvidia cofounder resigned as CEO last week after admitting he had an affair with Alice Huang, a Chinese businesswoman accused of having ties to Chinese intelligence services. Alice previously worked at the Singapore-based data center company Megaspeed, which offered remote access services and is suspected of engaging in chip smuggling.

The scandal may have been so embarrassing for the White House that officials felt compelled to demonstrate they had the situation under control. Apparently, the cheating scandal of the century was the motivation they were missing. (A White House spokesperson previously told WIRED that the newly introduced rule would “crack down on the smuggling of advanced US SI chips” and “help ensure that America’s most advanced chips go first to US SI innovators, not Chinese shell companies.”).

It has been revealed that it started in the fall of 2022, when the Biden administration unveiled a set of rules that would radically alter the future of AI and who was allowed to build it. The goal was to choke off China's access to the advanced chips needed to train the world's most powerful AI models, as well as the equipment required to manufacture those chips.

Sources indicate that it's worth remembering just how radical this approach was at the time. For decades, the US had used export controls to keep sensitive American technology away from specific military programs, governments, and blacklisted companies accused of carrying out human rights abuses. But the Biden administration was attempting something far more ambitious: using Washington's influence over the global semiconductor industry to hold back the world's second-largest economy from competing at the cutting edge of one of the most key newly introduced technologies in generations.

It has been revealed that the strategy rested on a relatively simple idea. Training the most advanced AI models requires enormous amounts of computing power, and American companies like Nvidia dominate the market for the chips that provide it. By restricting China's access to those chips, Washington hoped to preserve America's technological lead.

Four years later, the US certainly cannot claim total victory. But boy, have things gotten messy. Part of the problem is that Washington tasked the Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS), a relatively small, underfunded agency within the Commerce Department, with leading enforcement of the controls. The bureau had a budget of just $235 million in 2026—a paltry sum compared to what Nvidia rakes in in a single week.

Sources indicate that the bureau's job only got harder as the Biden administration introduced successive rounds of increasingly complex restrictions, scrambling to tighten the rules as chipmakers found increasingly elaborate ways to get around them. But one of the bureau's biggest challenges was fighting what became a booming industry for smuggling AI chips into China.

At BIS, Megaspeed has become a poster child for the problem, although it's far from the only firm suspected of involvement, or even the largest, according to a person familiar with the matter.

Recent findings suggest that according to Bloomberg, roughly 50,000 of the estimated 136,000 AI chips Megaspeed imported into Malaysia and Indonesia in 2024 and 2025 weren't accounted for in Nvidia's initial inventory checks. It's not clear where they may have ended up. (Nvidia later said it had found at least some of them.).

In a recent development, even if all of the unaccounted-for chips ended up in China, they would represent only a fraction of the advanced semiconductors believed to have been smuggled into the country over the past few years. Researchers at the Institute for Progress estimate that, by the end of 2026, China could have accumulated smuggled computing power equivalent to roughly 1 million of Nvidia's high-end H100 chips.

But all along, Chinese companies didn't necessarily need to smuggle chips into the country to use them. They could just rent computing power from data centers in other countries, and best of all, the practice didn’t violate US export controls. This wasn’t some hidden loophole—every policymaker and researcher who worked on the chip restrictions was deeply aware of it. So why let the practice continue?

It has been revealed that for one, renting computing power can be more expensive and cumbersome than owning the chips outright, especially for companies that need to train large AI models over long periods. Some analysts argued that allowing Chinese firms to use American technology overseas could help keep them dependent on it instead of pushing them to develop domestic alternatives. Restricting access would also be difficult to enforce and could hurt US technology companies.

Now, Washington is moving into this territory anyway. Monday's announcement represents another significant expansion of US efforts to control China's technological development. In 2022, Washington set out to prevent Chinese companies from acquiring certain American chips. Four years later, it’s trying to regulate how Chinese companies use those same chips, even when the hardware never enters China.

Whether that's a good idea depends partly on how much the original restrictions have actually accomplished.

There is evidence that export controls have made it considerably harder for Chinese AI companies to acquire the kind of computing power of their American competitors. But assessing the precise impact of the policies has proven to be extremely difficult.

This strategy comes with a lot of risks, and like with everything else in life, there are real winners and losers. For example, forcing US chip companies to cut off Chinese customers has come at a cost to American companies. In a study of earlier US export restrictions, researchers at the Federal Reserve Bank of New York found that affected American suppliers struggled to replace lost business in China with new customers elsewhere. They estimate that the restrictions wiped $130 billion from the companies’ combined market value, while also hurting their profitability and employment.

The restrictions have also given China a very powerful incentive to find ways to compete in AI without relying on American technology. Huawei, for example, developed a way to link powerful chips together to create larger, more powerful megachip systems. The Chinese AI lab DeepSeek proved to the world that finding ways to make training more efficient could help developers build competitive models with fewer resources.

I worry that the Trump administration will soon find that it has gotten out over its own skis. It’s now trying to control not only which chips Chinese companies can buy from American companies, but also how they can use American technology anywhere it may be in the world. I’m not sure that is the kind of responsibility I want to bestow on anyone in response to what happened in one person’s sex life.

Many gamers have already taken advantage of a sneaky little trick that allowed them to play the long-awaited Grand Theft Auto VI one day early on New Zealand time.

However, the vast majority of gamers in the U.S. are awaiting the official launch at midnight on Nov. 19. And in the hours ahead of the game's debut, some users are already reporting problems accessing the PlayStation Network. User error reports for PlayStation spiked on DownDetector around 2 p.m. ET on Nov. 18, and reports remained elevated into the evening.

The good news: The official PlayStation Service Status page shows that all systems are go for launch, as of this writing.

The question is: Will PlayStation and Xbox be able to handle all the millions of gamers trying to download and access the game all at once?

With so many different companies and services suffering from outages recently, gamers may be understandably nervous. And we have you covered. Here's how you can easily tell if PlayStation or Xbox is down — or if it's just you and your internet connection.

Catch up on the latest 'Grand Theft Auto VI' news and updates from Mashable.

If you run into any issues while trying to load up GTA 6 on your PlayStation, head over to the official PlayStation Service Status page. If there is a problem, you can also check the PlayStation Support account on X for updates.

These official resources will let you know at a glance whether Sony PlayStation services are up and running. And if there is an glitch, the status page will tell you which PlayStation service is having problems.

Again, as of publication, PlayStation's services are all up and running.

Remember: You'll need to update your PlayStation console before you can play GTA 6.

Microsoft has a similar status page for Xbox users. If you run into trouble trying to enter Vice City on GTA 6 launch day, simply head to the official Xbox status page.

This page will tell you if any Xbox services are having problems.

As of publication, Xbox's services are all up and running as well, despite some elevated activity on DownDetector.

Most marketing teams still measure visibility the same way they always have: rankings, click-through rates, and organic traffic. But buyers have moved on.

Search tools and AI engines now synthesize answers directly on the screen, creating a world of zero-click searches where your website is entirely bypassed.

According to recent reports, the “old days” are not coming back. The question for marketers is no longer, How do we rank first? It's How do we become part of the answer?

The answer isn't publishing more content; it’s making your knowledge impossible for AI to ignore.

It has been revealed that showing up is only half the battle. Where you appear inside an AI-generated response matters just as much.

Think about the experience. If your brand is mentioned after multiple answer cards, product recommendations, follow-up questions, and community discussions, most people will never see it. Ranking reports won't capture that.

According to recent reports, one way to think about this is pixel depth. Instead of measuring position on a search results page, measure how prominently your brand appears within the answer itself. Visibility increasingly depends on whether you're seen before someone feels they've learned enough to stop reading. It’s no longer enough to rank at the top of search results. Now “share of visibility” models also weigh SERP features, ads, and AI Overview presence for a more holistic view of what kind of attention your tech giant can expect to get.

Search engines were designed to index pages. Large language models work differently.

According to recent reports, rather than evaluating a page as a single unit, they connect facts, concepts, entities, and relationships from many sources to generate an answer. AI systems don’t treat pages as single units; they extract and recombine facts across sources. Your website becomes one source of evidence rather than the destination.

That changes what makes content valuable.

A polished landing page still matters for people. But before someone reaches that page, an AI system has already decided whether your information is clear, credible, and consistent enough to include in its response.

According to recent reports, many organizations approach answer engine optimization as a writing exercise. In reality, it starts much earlier.

Sources indicate that AI systems need information they can understand. That depends on consistent terminology, structured content, clear metadata, well-maintained documentation, and a single source of truth across product pages, help centers, blogs, and FAQs.

When the same product is described three different ways across your website, you create uncertainty. A customer might work through those inconsistencies. An AI system is more likely to move on to a source that's easier to interpret.

Kemberly Gong, VP of Marketing at Contentful, recently described what AI systems look for: structured content, clear context, authority, and validation from other trusted sources. AI doesn't automatically accept what your brand says about itself. It looks for consistency across your own content as well as supporting signals from reviews, documentation, industry publications, and community discussions.

The goal isn't simply to publish more content. It's to build a body of knowledge that holds together.

Clear writing has always been good for readers. Now it's also good for machines.

Recent findings suggest that descriptive headings, concise paragraphs, clearly defined terms, logical structure, and scannable formatting all make it easier for AI systems to understand and reference your content. Those same qualities make life easier for human readers.

Content that’s easy for answer engines to interpret shares four characteristics:.

Consistency: Use the same terminology across product pages, documentation, FAQs and blogs.

Clarity: Define technical terms the first time they’re introduced, and keep each section focused on a single idea.

Authority: Support your claims with original research, customer evidence, expert insights or other unique information.

Structure: Organize content with descriptive headings, a logical hierarchy and standalone sections that answer engines can easily interpret and reference.

Industry observers note that those principles don’t just improve readability. They also make your content easier for answer engines to interpret and include in AI-generated responses.

The web has no shortage of AI-generated summaries. What it lacks is information that exists nowhere else.

Original research. Customer data. Benchmarks. First-hand expertise. Strong opinions backed by experience. Those are the assets AI systems can't easily replace because they aren't available everywhere else.

That makes original thinking more valuable than ever.

When ten companies publish the same advice, AI has little reason to favor one over another. When your organization contributes something genuinely new, you become the source others reference.

Before investing in another AEO checklist, step back and ask:.

Could an AI accurately explain what our manufacturer does?

Do our product pages, documentation, and thought leadership describe the same concepts consistently?

Is our expertise organized well enough to be cited?

Are we contributing original knowledge or simply producing more content?

According to recent reports, strong brands aren't disappearing from AI answers because they lack expertise. They're disappearing because their expertise is fragmented, inconsistent, or difficult for machines to interpret.

The organizations that gain visibility over the next few years won't necessarily publish the most content. They'll make their knowledge easier to understand, easier to verify, and easier to trust. That's good for AI systems, and even better for the people reading the answers.

Review: Amazon’s Alexa Tablet 8 is a Fire Tablet with Google Play for $150 – what’s not to love?

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Amazon shocked everyone in October when it debuted its upcoming Alexa Tablet series with Google Play support built-in, addressing the biggest shortcoming of its older Fire Tablets.
  • The Alexa Tablet 8 is one of three latest Amazon tablets that rolled out in October with Google Play on board, and it’s also the one I was personally the most excited about.
  • Right up there with Amazon’s long-running reputation in the tablet space, Alexa Tablet 8 is very much an affordable device, and that’s reflected in its fairly meager specs:.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Amazon shocked everyone in October when it debuted its upcoming Alexa Tablet series with Google Play support built-in, addressing the biggest shortcoming of its older Fire Tablets. For Black Friday 2026, the Alexa Tablet 8 is a mere $150 and, with Google Play on board, this feels like a Fire Tablet that’s all grown up.

The Alexa Tablet 8 is one of three latest Amazon tablets that rolled out in October with Google Play on board, and it’s also the one I was personally the most excited about. I love a good tiny Android tablet, but there just aren’t that many out there – and some of the ones we do have are exorbitantly expensive.

Right up there with Amazon’s long-running reputation in the tablet space, Alexa Tablet 8 is very much an affordable device, and that’s reflected in its fairly meager specs:.

Yet, I didn’t find myself put off by the device.

I specifically asked Amazon for a review unit of the absolute base model – 4GB of RAM and lockscreen ads – and I can say with confidence it’s Not Bad at the end of the day.

The display is objectively not good, but it’s not really trying to be flashy either. The panel gets bright enough for most indoor use and, for general browsing or watching videos around the house or even on a flight, it gets the job done. If anything, my biggest complaint on the display was just how smudgey it gets with fingerprints.

In a recent development, hardware is a strong suit. The Alexa Tablet 8 has an aluminum build that comes in this gorgeous teal color as well as a softer “Rosette” pink (or “Graphite,” if you want to keep it boring). It’s thin and light and slips into a bag easily, and even fit into the back pocket of my jeans. Buttons are clicky and aspects such as the speakers actually do well enough – like the display, the speakers aren’t good, but they’re not bad by any stretch either.

In a recent development, amazon has a folio cover available that’s simple but nice, with a fabric finish that’s grippy. It’s an extra $40, though, which feels like a bit much for a super-affordable Android slate.

The biggest question was around the software experience, and this is where this upcoming effort really shines.

Recent findings suggest that alexa Tablet 8 ships with Android 16 out of the box, not FireOS or whatever Amazon was calling its forked experience on Fire Tablets (I genuinely refuse to go double-check because it’s a memory I’m thrilled to never have to revisit). It’s a pretty “stock” experience, with Amazon leaving aspects such as the notification shade/quick settings alone, and even the Settings menu feels pretty clean.

That’s not to say nothing has changed. The homescreen has a fairly standard layout , but with these neat little corner widgets – one a “dynamic” widget with scrolling content (mostly ads) and the other a shortcut for Alexa search. Amazon is pushing Alexa as a voice assistant pretty heavily on these tablets, but I’m happy to report it’s pretty easy to ignore if you choose. These tablets will be great additions to your Alexa ecosystem if you’re invested, but I’m simply not.

In a recent development, the biggest change you’ll find is the lockscreen, where Amazon’s base models all come with lockscreen ads. This saves you about $20 on the hardware, and it’s not that bad of an experience. That said, I’d absolutely spend the extra $20 at purchase to go without them, especially seeing as this blocks the ability to set a lockscreen wallpaper at all. It doesn’t cost anything more to remove them later, though, with a $20 charge through your Amazon account removing ads.

But what’s notable here is that, for the fire time, Amazon is admitting defeat and installing the Google Play Store.

Sources indicate that alexa Tablet 8, and the rest of the lineup, has Google Play out of the box and access to any app you want. This means that you can, if you choose, fully ignore Amazon’s own services and do whatever you want. The smallest of examples: While Amazon’s built-in keyboard is fine, it’s wonderful that I don’t have to jump through hoops to switch over to Gboard. Fire Tablets were always an enticing value with a significant catch, but Amazon’s change in this regard truly makes Alexa Tablets an attractive option for everyone – not just those willing to put up with the restriction or put in the work to hack Google apps on board.

It has been revealed that performance, despite the meager specs, is not awful. MediaTek’s low-end chip has just enough horsepower for general use, and 4GB of RAM isn’t as detrimental as I would have expected. It’s not fast by any means, but you could do a lot worse. There are 4GB Android tablets I’ve literally decided not to review because I couldn’t use them past the setup process, so the fact that Amazon is delivering a completely usable experience is a win in my book, even more so that I don’t actually mind using it. There’s a caveat to that, of course, and it’s that you shouldn’t expect to do a ton on this base model. For light browsing, reading Kindle books (or whatever other reading app since, you know, Google Play), or watching videos, this is great. For games, you’ll want to look elsewhere (and expect to spend more).

“Not awful” is kind of the pattern here.

Alexa Tablet 8 isn’t some shining example of a perfect budget tablet, but I think it really nails the fundamentals. At its usual $230~ starting price, it’s a plenty-good deal for those in the market for an affordable Android slate, but the Black Friday pricing of just $150 is all the better – I just wish the model with 8GB of RAM was also on sale.

Sources indicate that amazon’s pivot to Alexa Tablets is great – though I hope the company knows full well that everyone is still going to call these Fire Tablets or Kindles or whatever combination of brands that spring to mind. But that reputation might work in Amazon’s favor at the end of the day. While there’s a huge portion of the audience that’s been left frustrated for years at the lack of Play Store support on Fire Tablets, they’ve still been a market success for the most part, so this shift is just a win for everyone. Users get a better experience, Amazon gets to shuffle its priorities away from a dead app store, and the market as a whole gets an affordable piece of hardware that doesn’t suck.

  • At the IPO price, Anthropic is reportedly valued at $1.5 trillion on a fully diluted basis, a significant increase from the $965 billion the manufacturer reached in May when it raised $65 billion in its last private market round, but below the $2 trillion it was reportedly aiming for several months ago.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Anthropic has reportedly priced its long-awaited IPO at $83 per share, above its initial range of $70 to $78, signaling strong investor appetite for one of the companies at the center of the AI boom, despite market jitters following the departure of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, which shook confidence in the industry.

At the IPO price, Anthropic is reportedly valued at $1.5 trillion on a fully diluted basis, a significant increase from the $965 billion the manufacturer reached in May when it raised $65 billion in its last private market round, but below the $2 trillion it was reportedly aiming for several months ago.

Anthropic will begin its life as a public tech giant on Thursday, trading on Nasdaq under the ticker symbol “ANT.” A strong first day of trading would signal that investors remain optimistic about AI adoption, despite recent volatility in AI-driven stocks.

The company’s performance is expected to set expectations for private AI companies, including Anthropic’s main rival OpenAI, which was last reportedly valued at $1.25 billion but has yet to announce intends for an IPO.

Although none of Anthropic’s venture capital investors holds more than a 5% stake in the organization, the IPO is a massive windfall for its numerous backers. Investors that own approximately 1% of the company reportedly include Sequoia and former Google CEO Eric Schmidt. Singaporean sovereign wealth fund GIC also holds about a 1% stake in the company, according to a person familiar with the matter. Other backers set to make billions are Iconiq, Menlo Ventures, Coatue, and Sound Ventures, a firm introduced by Guy Oseary and actor Ashton Kutcher, and Spark Ventures, the only VC firm known to hold a board seat at the company.

Some of the company’s existing investors, namely Sequoia, Iconiq, Lightspeed, Accel, and Altimeter Capital Management, are so enthusiastic about Anthropic’s future that they were reportedly planning to buy billions of dollars’ worth of the company’s shares in the IPO.

In a recent development, yet the investors’ holdings in Anthropic pale in comparison to those of the Claude maker’s strategic partners, Amazon, which owns nearly 15% of the firm, and Google, which holds almost 14%. A group of major tech companies, including AMD, Broadcom, Google, Micron, Microsoft, Nvidia, and TSMC Partners, have also agreed to purchase $26 billion worth of non-voting shares through a private placement alongside the IPO.

The manufacturer’s seven co-founders, including CEO Dario Amodei, each sold nearly 3.4 million shares in the IPO, according to the S-1 filing, bringing in about $282 million for each.

Latest Update: Apple among the companies facing pressure from US senators over ‘nudify’ apps

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The Guardian reports that three US senators have sent letters to the CEOs of Apple, Google, and Meta, demanding answers about their failure to prevent access to AI-powered ‘nudify’ apps.
  • Last month, Apple updated its App Store rules in an attempt to crack down on apps that enable owners to generate nonconsensual nude images.
  • According to the updated rules, apps that allow people to create AI-generated content must include safeguards against abuse, including tools to filter objectionable material, report offensive content, and block abusive users.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Guardian reports that three US senators have sent letters to the CEOs of Apple, Google, and Meta, demanding answers about their failure to prevent access to AI-powered ‘nudify’ apps. Here are the details.

Last month, Apple updated its App Store rules in an attempt to crack down on apps that enable owners to generate nonconsensual nude images.

According to the updated rules, apps that allow people to create AI-generated content must include safeguards against abuse, including tools to filter objectionable material, report offensive content, and block abusive users.

Apple also warns that apps used primarily for pornographic content or the objectification of real people may be removed from the App Store without notice.

While definitely well-intended, Apple’s changes came amid growing reports of AI-powered nudify apps, which easily allow users to generate nonconsensual intimate images.

Two months before these changes, Apple removed an app that allowed users to create pornographic deepfakes of real people after WIRED reached out for comment, which in turn came one month after San Francisco City Attorney David Chiu demanded that Apple and Google remove several nudify apps from their app stores.

Apple also removed several apps following investigations by the Tech Transparency Project (TTP), which published reports in January and April revealing that such apps were widely available on the App Store, sometimes even appearing in sponsored search results.

Throughout these investigations, Apple has maintained that nudify apps have always been prohibited under its App Review Guidelines, and that it proactively rejects and removes apps that violate its policies, including those flagged through user reports.

Apple, of course, is not alone in this challenge, with Google facing similar criticism over their availability on the Play Store, and Meta coming under scrutiny for allowing developers to advertise these apps on Facebook and Instagram, as highlighted in the WIRED report mentioned above.

Which brings us to today’s report from The Guardian.

According to The Guardian’s exclusive report, “three Senate Democrats sent letters to tech CEOs saying safeguards against nudification apps are insufficient on their platforms.”.

Industry observers note that A trio of US Senators say Apple and Google are failing to effectively detect and remove apps that can be used to generate nonconsensual nude or pornographic imagery. They also say Meta is continuing to profit off of ads for these so-called nudification apps that “victimize women and girls worldwide”.

The senators, namely Ron Wyden of Oregon, Ed Markey of Massachusetts, and Ben Luján of New Mexico, claim that in addition to failing to remove these apps, the companies may actually be profiting from their distribution and promotion.

Commenting on the letter, both Google and Meta remarked they prohibit such apps or their promotion and work to detect and remove violations from their platforms, broadly echoing what Apple has repeatedly stated when reached for comment in the past over these same issues.

However, Wyden’s office argues that simply reaffirming, or in Apple’s case, updating these policies, means little if the companies continue to struggle to enforce them.

Keith Chu, the chief communications adviser and deputy policy director to Wyden, noted that clarifying policies is not the same thing as enforcing them. Despite the companies reaffirming the prohibition of these apps, they continue to proliferate across Apple and Google app stores or be promoted in ads on Meta platforms, he added.

In its latest investigation, published just last month, TTP found 135 apps capable of generating nude or pornographic imagery on the App Store and the Play Store, using accounts registered to 13-year-old boys.

Additionally, researchers found that even accounts configured with parental controls were able to download these apps without requiring parental approval.

Despite Apple and Google removing the apps identified in the investigation, The Guardian noted that these apps continued to work on devices where they had already been installed.

Now, Senator Wyden warns that Congress may need to step in if the companies fail to do a better job of cracking down on these apps.
