#1136. Xreal Aura review: Solid AR glasses hampered by Google's half-baked Android XR

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 10m • 📚 Deep Dive (1949 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Engadget ↗ Open Full Page

Xreal Aura review: Solid AR glasses hampered by Google's half-baked Android XR

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (1949 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Engadget

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Two years after Google revealed Android XR, and a year after Samsung's flagship $1,800 Galaxy XR headset landed with a fizzle, Google's latest stab at mixed reality is finally starting to seem...
  • Sources indicate that much like the baffling launch of Googlebooks, though, I'm not yet convinced that solid hardware will be able to save an ecosystem that Google isn't truly committed to.
  • According to recent reports, still, the Xreal Aura is a sign that Android XR hardware is more than just vaporware, and it's significantly cheaper than last year's Galaxy XR.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

For $1,099, we should expect more.

Two years after Google revealed Android XR, and a year after Samsung's flagship $1,800 Galaxy XR headset landed with a fizzle, Google's latest stab at mixed reality is finally starting to seem... real. We've taken a look at the first batch of Android XR smart glasses, which are landing this fall and take aim at Meta's popular Ray-Ban smart frames. Now Xreal is launching its Aura XR headset, which is the most intriguing Android XR device we've seen yet. It builds on Xreal's impressive history of virtual display glasses, adding just enough smarts to make it a viable, and far cheaper, alternative to Apple's Vision Pro. But with a starting price of $1,279 (on sale for $1,099 through December), it's still mainly targeted at VR developers.

Sources indicate that much like the baffling launch of Googlebooks, though, I'm not yet convinced that solid hardware will be able to save an ecosystem that Google isn't truly committed to. It's taken the manufacturer several years to actually deliver Android XR devices most people can actually afford, and there still aren't many notable apps that truly show off what the platform can do. Making Google Maps more immersive isn't enough.

According to recent reports, still, the Xreal Aura is a sign that Android XR hardware is more than just vaporware, and it's significantly cheaper than last year's Galaxy XR. It's also a glimpse of what we'll see with the upcoming Meta VR Glasses, and perhaps a sign of how Apple could actually follow up on the promise of the Vision Pro.

Sources indicate that the Xreal Aura is essentially a souped-up version of the firm's already excellent display glasses, except it's connected to a wired Compute Puck that houses all of the hardware necessary to run Android XR. The Aura's sunglasses-like frames look almost the same as the Xreal One Pro, except it also features cameras for spatial sensing, finger tracking and capturing photos and video. Xreal's transparent frames let you easily see the world around you, without the need for complicated camera pass-through functionality like the Galaxy XR and Apple Vision Pro use. You can also darken the screen to completely black out the world, similar to what you'd see on a typical VR headset.

Sources indicate that like Xreal's previous display glasses, the Aura relies on tiny micro-OLED screens with a resolution slightly beyond 1080p (1,920 by 1,200). They can reach up to 1,058 nits of brightness, which is slightly less than the 1,200 nits on the fresh Xreal One Pro+, and they support up to a 120Hz resolution with external devices. (The Android XR interface only runs at 72Hz.) The Aura's 70-degree field of view (FOV) is the best we've seen from Xreal, but it's also well below what we've seen on dedicated VR headsets, which use larger screens to completely fill your vision. The Apple Vision Pro reaches a FOV of around 100 degrees, while the Meta Quest 3 and many other headsets reach up to 110 degrees.

Industry observers note that for processing power, the Compute Puck houses a Qualcomm Snapdragon Reality Elite system-on-a-chip, and either 12GB or 16GB of RAM (alongside either 256GB or 512GB of storage). It also features Xreal's custom X1S spatial processor, a slightly improved version of the X1 chip on earlier frames, and it looks similar to the Vision Pro's battery pack. It has two USB-C ports, one for connecting to the Aura's frames and the other for either charging or connecting to a separate device. The top portion of the Compute Puck also serves as a trackpad, which is helpful for navigating Android XR without holding your hand up.

According to recent reports, when you plug in another device into the Compute Puck, its video output indicates up in a single Android XR window, which you can resize at will (and also position alongside other Android XR apps). You can also plug the Aura's frames directly into computers and other devices, where it functions exactly like the company's previous display glasses. That could be useful when you just need a significant virtual screen, and you don't want to deal with the hassle of juggling the Compute Puck.

According to recent reports, the Xreal Aura is exceptionally comfortable to wear; the frames weigh just 95 grams (0.2 pounds) on their own, compared to the 1.6-pound Vision Pro. The Aura is also fantastic for watching movies on a gigantic virtual display and it's incredibly useful if you need a large virtual monitor. But it's also crystal clear that Android XR is still in its infancy, as there aren't many notable apps to show off the platform. Using Android XR also doesn't feel very different than using any other Android device — as if Google made very little effort to reshape its OS around mixed reality. (There are definitely shades of the same laziness that annoyed me with Googlebooks.).

It doesn't help that apps crash often in Android XR, or that its core hand recognition interface feels lackluster. The Xreal Aura is often slow to respond to where my finger is pointing, or recognize when I'm pinching my fingers to select something. That's annoying enough when simply navigating Chrome or YouTube, but it's infuriating when trying to play an XR game like Cubism, which relies on placing 3D blocks in very specific places. Pointing at everything just to navigate Android XR also gets tiring over time — there's no eye-tracking like on the Vision Pro, which makes selecting on-screen elements a cinch. I promptly grew to prefer navigating Android XR with the Compute Puck's trackpad instead of pointing at everything.

Recent findings suggest that I was able to sit back and actually enjoy the Xreal Aura while watching the opening of Casino Royale on Prime Video, as well as a few episodes of the newly introduced Ghost in the Shell series. Xreal's micro-OLED displays deliver vibrant and colorful video, and its speakers built into the Aura's thick frames sound great. The Aura is also an excellent companion for laptops: I was able to have a giant screen mirroring my MacBook Air while playing the YouTube app right beside it.

Sources indicate that still, I wish there was more to actually do in Android XR. Zooming around the world in Google Maps' immersive view is fun, and I appreciated revisiting VR experiences like Cosmos Unseen: Black Holes, but they're not as enthralling as they are in traditional VR headsets. Being able to see the outside world easily is both a blessing and a curse on the Xreal Aura. You can also see spatial versions of pictures in the Google Photos app, which is cool at first, but promptly starts to feel gimmicky. Similarly, I didn't see much point to Android XR's Spatial Mode, which converts everything you see into pseudo-3D. It just gave me a headache while browsing the web.

According to recent reports, third-party support is clearly lackluster, especially when it comes to entertainment apps. All I saw was HBO Max and Prime Video, no Disney+ or Netflix (which isn't on visionOS, to be fair). You'll have to watch all of your other streaming services through Chrome, which isn't exactly a premium experience. It's also a particularly bad look when Meta just recently launched 3D movie support (including within the Disney+ app) on the Quest 3, 3S and its upcoming VR Glasses. That's something Google could eventually bring to Android XR, but who knows when that will happen.

Even the first-party YouTube app is a disappointment. There's a specific section for immersive videos, but it's filled with the same blurry 360-degree content we've been seeing for years. There's no substantial push for higher-resolution 180-degree 3D video like we've seen on the Vision Pro, or that Meta has declared for its VR Glasses.

Android XR is such a barren landscape, I sometimes found it more useful to just directly connect the Xreal Aura to my laptop or phone. At that point, it acts purely as a virtual display, but I found it helpful when I just wanted to stream a TV show in a crowded or tight space. The downside here is that connecting another device to the Compute Puck involves juggling a second USB-C cable, which can easily become frustrating. The Vision Pro can wirelessly connect to Macs, so it manages to avoid this issue.

Without the baggage of Android XR, the Xreal Aura was also able to deliver a brighter and sharper virtual view of my MacBook Air's desktop. There's a slight blurriness to external devices when using the Compute Puck, which makes text difficult to read. That's not a problem when you're directly connected to the glasses. But if that's the case, why not just get some of Xreal's existing display glasses? (More on this below.).

It has been revealed that battery life is another potentially worrying variable. The Aura's battery drained from full to 40 percent after just 90 minutes of watching Prime Video content, browsing the web and messing around with Google Map's immersive view. It lasted for another 95 minutes before it completely drained down as I caught up on Ghost in the Shell.

The Compute Puck's heat output was also very noticeable. Its tiny fan often felt like it was working hard to cool down the device, and I was worried about stuffing it into my pocket like I do with the Vision Pro's battery pack. Xreal recommends avoiding pockets and other enclosed spaces while the Aura is doing serious work or fast charging. That's likely why the firm bundles a lanyard and belt holster in the Aura's box.

Since the Xreal Aura also features prominent cameras, I hesitated about using it in public spaces, where people might mistake it for Meta's Ray-Ban "pervert glasses." That's an issue the manufacturer's cheaper display glasses avoid completely as they're camera-free (unless you add an additional accessory). I could just point to those specs and tell any worried coffee shop neighbor they don't have a camera.

According to recent reports, unless you're a VR developer keen to get a leg up on Android XR, there's no reason to buy the Xreal Aura. At its $1,099 sale price (or the eventual $1,279 standard price), it comes in far cheaper than the $1,800 Galaxy XR or $3,699 Vision Pro, but the handful of games and immersive apps for Android XR still don't justify its cost.

Sources indicate that it's a particularly bad investment since we don't know how long Google will actually stick with Android XR. Don't forget that its earlier attempts at VR, like Google Cardboard and Daydream, all died after a few years of lackluster support. Given that Android XR also encompasses simpler smart glasses, and that Meta is working hard to dominate this market, I'd hope Google would give it a few years to find some footing.

Recent findings suggest that and if the simple idea of having a virtual screen on your face sounds intriguing, then consider Xreal's existing display glasses. I loved the Xreal One last year, and the firm just recently rolled out a brighter One+ model for $600. Even the $299 Xreal XBX a01+ specs were bright and fun to use, even though they don't support any spatial features.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • It has been revealed that if you buy something from a link, The Verge may earn a commission.
  • Facing opposition at home, Trump is eyeing the former US colony to build chip fabs and data centers.

Industry observers note that president Donald Trump was greeted by no less than five beauty queens when he landed in the Philippines on Tuesday, according to local news outlet Rappler. As he stepped onto the tarmac, a child handed him small US and Philippine flags. A band played “YMCA,” a staple at Trump rallies, as more girls in traditional bell-sleeved blouses and young men in wide-brimmed hats danced to the song.

Outside the airport, hundreds of protesters packed streets bearing signs — and at least one prop casket — saying “Trump out.” Others say “Reject Pax Silica,” the name for the US-led international initiative to secure chips and critical minerals used in the hardware fueling the AI boom.

“Pax” comes from the Latin word for “peace, stability, and long-term prosperity,” the Pax Silica website proudly says. Yet the unspoken question — peace and prosperity for whom? — explains the whiplash between the Philippine government’s warm welcome of Trump and the public fury raging outside.

Industry observers note that trump states he wants to “win AI” — whatever that means. As such, the US needs data centers full of GPUs to do it. With Americans increasingly opposed to data centers and chip factories being built in their communities, the US is now recruiting less affluent nations to take up some of the slack. Lawmakers from both the US and the Philippines are promising a slice of the riches that advances in generative AI are supposed to create. And that’s supposed to be worth the land razed, homes destroyed, and natural resources lost in the name of technological progress. In the Philippines, that’s taking the shape of a proposed 1,620-hectare (4,000 acres) hub for chip factories, processing plants for critical minerals, and data centers.

It has been revealed that at least two dozen countries have signed on to the Pax Silica initiative, and Trump was expected to pressure more to join while in the Philippines for events related to the Association of Southeast Asian Nations summit. With Pax Silica, the US aims to insulate itself from China’s dominance in manufacturing semiconductors and processing critical minerals needed to make those chips. Trump held a bilateral meeting with President Ferdinand R. Marcos Jr. Wednesday before heading to Shenzhen to meet with China’s President Xi Jinping and Russia’s President Vladimir Putin.

Philippine and US officials are expected to sign a framework agreement by the end of the year for the jointly developed Pax Silica Economic Security Zone. The details are still murky and shrouded in NDAs. The Philippines’ Bases Conversion and Development Authority (BCDA) overseeing the strategy expects an economic boom from minerals processing and chip manufacturing, with perhaps a data center or two on site. Meanwhile, human rights advocates who oppose the project warn that it will displace Indigenous residents, cutting them off from water resources on which they rely.

“How do we give up our burial grounds, our church, our livelihood?”.

“We do not want to give up our community,” Petronila Capiz-Muñoz, chieftain of the Indigenous Aeta Hungey tribe, told Human Rights Watch. “How do we give up our burial grounds, our church, our livelihood? This is where we source our water, this is where we plant.” Capiz-Muñoz said BCDA officials have told residents that they’ll need to relocate by December to make way for development. Small farmers are also afraid the semiconductor hub will push them off their lands, according to Lian Buan, Southeast Asia researcher at Human Rights Watch.

There are layers of land-grabbing to unpack here.

The Aeta are among the first people to inhabit the Philippines, believed to have arrived around 30,000 years ago. And yet the Aeta Hungey tribe has been trying since 1994 to secure an official certificate recognizing its ancestral domain in one of the areas now facing industrial development. But since the tribe hasn’t been granted that certificate, the BCDA can still claim the AI hub will be built “outside titled ancestral domains.”.

According to recent reports, the agency notes the project will be on public land located at the former Clark Air Base built in the early 1900s when the Philippines was a US territory. The Philippine constitution now only allows its own citizens to own private land. But the BCDA can offer leases lasting as long as 99 years to foreign developers. The agency expects to rake in close to $1 billion USD (about 60 billion in PHP Peso) from lease income over the first 25 years.

There are layers of land-grabbing to unpack here.

The BCDA was in talks with around 30 different companies interested in setting up shop in Clark’s proposed AI hub, then-BCDA President and CEO Joshua Bingcang told reporters in July. He couldn’t name names, he mentioned, because of NDAs — creating the same kind of opacity that has turned Americans against data centers on their home turf.

Industry observers note that he did mention, however, that an American energy firm was conducting a feasibility study into building a liquefied natural gas (LNG) line and plant to meet the hub’s enormous electricity demand. Bingcang called LNG a clean fuel, but that’s provably false. LNG is primarily methane, a smog-forming pollutant that is an even more potent greenhouse gas than carbon dioxide.

Bingcang mentioned in September that the Philippine government wanted to invite Nvidia, TSMC, and Apple. While one or two data center developers had expressed interest, according to Bingcang, most of the companies interested were “high tech” manufacturing firms. He has also described chip manufacturing as a “clean” industry, echoing corporate spin that’s been around since the start of Silicon Valley.

Industry observers note that at the first chip fabs in California, workers — many of them Filipino immigrants — donned “bunny suits” to assemble sensitive chips in environmentally controlled “clean rooms.” Little did they know that the gear they wore offered little protection against the harsh chemicals used in manufacturing, which also leaked out of storage tanks to contaminate soil and groundwater. When studies came out in the ’90s documenting disproportionately high rates of miscarriages among workers, companies pledged to phase out some of the chemicals linked to reproductive health risks. Around the same time, chip manufacturing started to move out of the US to Asia, where similar health problems stemming from the same chemicals cropped up even decades later.

Chipmakers say their fabs have gotten much safer over the years, in part because more work is automated. Even so, the BCDA estimates that the AI hub will create up to 190,000 direct jobs. The BCDA, White House, and Philippine’s Malacañang Palace did not immediately respond to questions from The Verge.

“I don’t want to date myself, but I knew your parents very well. They were great,” Trump told President Marcos during his visit. Marcos’ parents are estimated to have stolen up to $30 billion from government coffers over decades of rule before a people power movement ousted the current president’s father from the same office in the 1980s. But public memory, it seems, can be short.

Industry observers note that and skyrocketing demand for more powerful chips used for generative AI has raised fears among environmental and labor groups that history might repeat itself. Companies move fast and break things, leaving a toxic mess in their wake. And when Americans decide they’ve had enough in their own back yards, the industry sets up shop somewhere else where they think their customers aren’t paying attention and politicians are happy to look the other direction.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Interim Nvidia CEO Colette Kress told employees "let's move forward" on Wednesday during the manufacturer's first all-hands meeting since founder Jensen Huang resigned, according to an attendee who spoke to CNBC on the condition of anonymity.

Kress was joined by newly appointed board chair Harvey Jones and hyperscale and high-performance computing head Ian Buck.

Several other senior members of Nvidia's executive team spoke or joined Kress on stage, including longtime company veteran Jeff Fisher, SVP of software engineering Dwight Diercks, senior vice president of GPU engineering Jonah Alben, executive vice president in charge of operations Debora Shoquist and co-founder Chris Malachowsky, according to people familiar with the matter.

Kress opened with the message about moving forward and also mentioned pay raises and explained that the yearly review process would be moved up from March to December when employees typically get a pay raise and are granted more stock. Nvidia shares are down 37% from its 52-week high.

In a recent development, jones discussed the search for the next CEO, the attendee added. The meeting lasted about an hour and was in person as well as streamed on Microsoft Teams.

Sources indicate that the general sentiment swirling in the room, according to the attendee, was that employees want Huang to come back. Employees have spoken up on X in recent days to call for the return of Huang as CEO, and one senior employee reportedly sent a letter to the board warning Nvidia would lose "irreplaceable talent" if it doesn't consider reinstating Huang.

But another person familiar with the matter disagreed, saying that employees welcomed the remarks from leadership as well as the visibility into company leadership.

"The Nvidia board unanimously accepted his resignation and does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO," Jones said during the earnings call on Tuesday.

Sources indicate that some executives shared that they do not agree with Jones. "Why make such a strong definitive statement when the investigation is still playing out," an employee told CNBC. The employee asked not to be named given the sensitivity of the subject.

The meeting comes one day after former CEO Huang remarked he was ready to return as CEO should the board want him. Multiple employees told CNBC that Huang's letter "fired employees up.".

It has been revealed that despite recent turmoil, Wednesday's meeting was not out of the ordinary. Nvidia typically holds all-hands the morning after quarterly earnings reports, according to a former employee who spoke to CNBC on the condition of anonymity. Kress recapped Tuesday's earnings report, calling it a "great quarter," according to one person familiar with the matter.

In past meetings, Huang took time to answer questions submitted by employees, according to the former employee. A person in the room told CNBC that the executives did not answer questions in Wednesday's all-hands.

Nvidia shares were down Wednesday, a day after the tech giant reported third-quarter earnings that topped Wall Street expectations and gave no signal that the company was going to slow its growth.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • For a lot of folks, Grand Theft Auto VI is an excuse to live out the life of a powerful criminal, or at least try to be the world's best virtual boyfriend.
  • Sources indicate that GTA 6 seems to be defined as much by its embrace of the mundane as anything else.
  • It has been revealed that one feature that some early GTA 6 launch coverage has highlighted is the ability for the protagonist Jason to fix up his house.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

For a lot of folks, Grand Theft Auto VI is an excuse to live out the life of a powerful criminal, or at least try to be the world's best virtual boyfriend. But for those of us who left the "rampaging through the streets in a tank" days behind us, it sounds like the game has a lot more to offer.

Sources indicate that GTA 6 seems to be defined as much by its embrace of the mundane as anything else. Early reviews and Rockstar's previews have highlighted some of the seemingly countless, completely boring activities in the game. There are plenty of clips making the rounds, too, and with AI making fake gameplay easier to pass off as the real thing, we can't verify every video out there. Still, I’ve seen enough to know what I’ll be doing while everyone else is on their crime sprees.

It has been revealed that one feature that some early GTA 6 launch coverage has highlighted is the ability for the protagonist Jason to fix up his house. This doesn't just have cosmetic benefits. Doing repairs can also earn Jason some goodwill with Lucia, his partner in crime and love interest.

In a recent development, that means part of GTA 6's story will involve fixing a leaky roof, repairing a porch railing and stairs, and perhaps most excitingly, painting a bedroom wall. Yes, you can literally watch paint dry in GTA 6. This is what I've always wanted.

Developer Rockstar Games has become especially good at rendering the natural world in its more recent games, and it sounds like GTA 6 takes this to the next level. One major example of that is that you can devote your time to bird-watching, if you want.

There are apparently 62 different kinds of birds in the game, and you can check them out with a pair of binoculars before recording them in a wildlife logbook. I'm not joking when I say I know at least one person in real life who will absolutely go through the effort of finding all 62 birds. Heck, I might do it, too.

Recent findings suggest that one of my favorite real-life pastimes is staring at my phone for way too much of every day. Constantly switching between and refreshing the same three social media apps is sorta like putting my brain in a microwave, and I just can't stop doing it.

It has been revealed that that's why I'm excited about the prospect of literally doing the same thing in GTA 6. You can sit in bed and just look at fake social media apps, which is genuinely probably a better and healthier use of time than looking at real ones.

Dogs are wonderful. I love dogs, and I'm glad that petting them has become an expected mechanic in so many video games in recent years. The fact that you can pet dogs in GTA 6 is old news at this point.

It has been revealed that but I'm also a lifelong cat guy, and video games don't give cats nearly as much attention. Rockstar must have read my mind because you can totally pet cats in GTA 6.

You can bet your bottom dollar that I'll be doing that instead of robbing convenience stores.

In a recent development, previous GTA games have given players the ability to watch things on TV. I'm old enough to remember watching Katt Williams do virtual stand-up in GTA 4, for example.

But GTA 6 steps that up by introducing an original cartoon series called Macca & Friends that you can apparently watch entirely in-game. That is stupid enough that I might actually do it.

Sources indicate that last but certainly not least, there is one optional side activity that every good video game ought to have: fishing. And guess what? You can totally fish in GTA 6.

Sources indicate that what else needs to be said? Few things are more relaxing in real life and in virtual life than sitting back and doing some dang angling. I might crack open a cold one while doing this for maximum effect.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, meta’s newest AI model Muse Spark 1.3, unveiled yesterday, is faster and more performant on third-party benchmarks than its predecessor — with a caveat.
  • Meta’s newest AI model Muse Spark 1.3, unveiled yesterday, is faster and more performant on third-party benchmarks than its predecessor — with a caveat.
  • "Muse Spark 1.3 is rolling out today with frontier performance almost too cheap to meter," Meta co-founder and CEO Mark Zuckerberg wrote on X, calling it Meta’s “biggest jump” yet in coding and agentic work.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, meta’s newest AI model Muse Spark 1.3, unveiled yesterday, is faster and more performant on third-party benchmarks than its predecessor — with a caveat. "Muse Spark 1.3 is rolling out today with frontier performance almost too cheap to meter," Meta co-founder and CEO Mark Zuckerberg wrote on X, calling it Meta’s “biggest jump” yet in coding and agentic work.There is substance behind both parts of that claim. Muse Spark 1.3 makes significant gains over last month’s 1.2 release, particularly on long-running agent tasks. The version developers can access now is also one of the strongest price-performance offerings near the top of independent model rankings.Meta’s strongest Muse Spark 1.3 benchmark results come from its max reasoning configuration. Meta says that version is still completing additional safety testing and will arrive “shortly”; the third-party benchmarking firm Artificial Analysis says it evaluated max in a limited partner preview, and currently lists no API provider at all for the configuration. The version broadly rolling out this week through its Muse Code harness and the Meta Model API uses Meta’s previously available reasoning settings, including xhigh.That makes the more relevant enterprise question not whether Muse Spark 1.3 can reach frontier territory, but how close the model companies can actually deploy today gets — and at what real cost.The shipping model is very good, but not the benchmark leaderMeta does disclose results for both configurations in its underlying evaluation report, so this is not a case of the manufacturer hiding the deployable model. But its launch materials prominently showcase the max variant, and some of the largest scores belong to that configuration.For example, Meta reports GDPval-AA v2 scores of 1,754 Elo for max versus 1,709 for xhigh, OSWorld 2.0 scores of 66.9 versus 57.2, and JobBench scores of 64.9 versus 61.2. On some tests the distinction is negligible or reversed: DeepSearchQA is tied at 89.4, while xhigh scores 89.2 on Terminal-Bench 2.1 versus max at 88.8.Artificial Analysis scores Muse Spark 1.3 max at 62 on its Intelligence Index and the shipping xhigh version at 61. The latter ties GPT-5.6 Sol max, Grok 4.6 high and Claude Opus 5 high. But Anthropic still occupies the top of the leaderboard: Claude Fable 5.1 reaches 66 at max and 65 at xhigh, while Claude Opus 5 reaches 63 at max and xhigh.In other words, Muse Spark 1.3 xhigh is legitimately in the frontier cluster, but it is not the model currently setting the frontier.That is still a substantial change from Muse Spark 1.2. VentureBeat’s coverage of last month’s launch found Meta fielding a credible coding challenger that nevertheless generally trailed Anthropic’s best model. Muse Spark 1.2 scored 82.9% on Terminal-Bench 2.1 versus Opus 5’s 86.7%, and also finished behind Opus on the other main coding comparisons Meta presented.With 1.3, Meta is no longer merely showing up in that contest. On several coding and agentic evaluations, it is trading wins with OpenAI and Anthropic.Meta says the underlying model has also become easier to operate. Muse Spark 1.3 is trained to maintain multiple workflows in a long thread, gather context with tools, detect gaps in its own prepares, ask users for clarification when necessary and confirm before consequential actions. In Meta engineers’ internal comparisons, it used roughly 20% fewer tool calls and 25% fewer tokens than 1.2 during coding work.For enterprises paying for thousands or millions of agent loops, those behavioral improvements could matter more than another leaderboard point.‘Almost too cheap to meter’ does not mean Meta cut its pricesMuse Spark 1.3 did not receive an API price cut. Meta kept Standard pricing exactly where it was for Muse Spark 1.2: $1.25 per million input tokens, $4.25 per million output tokens and $0.15 per million cached input tokens.ModelInput ($/1M)Output ($/1M)Total ($/1M)SourceMuse Spark 1.2 / 1.3 Contributor$0.10$0.20$0.30MetaMiMo-V2.5 Flash$0.10$0.30$0.40XiaomiDeepSeek-V4-Flash — off-peak$0.22$0.66$0.88DeepSeekGPT-5.6 Luna$0.20$1.20$1.40OpenAIMiniMax-M3$0.30$1.20$1.50MiniMaxLongCat-2.0 — limited-time promo$0.30$1.20$1.50LongCatDeepSeek-V4-Flash — peak hours$0.44$1.32$1.76DeepSeekMiMo-V2.5$0.40$2.00$2.40XiaomiDeepSeek-V4-Pro — off-peak$0.66$1.98$2.64DeepSeekLongCat-2.0 — standard$0.75$2.95$3.70LongCatMiMo-V2.5 Pro (≤256K)$1.00$3.00$4.00XiaomiGemini 3.7 Flash — through Dec. 31, 2026$0.75$3.75$4.50GoogleGemini 3.8 Flash — through Dec. 31, 2026$0.75$3.75$4.50GoogleDeepSeek-V4-Pro — peak hours$1.32$3.96$5.28DeepSeekMuse Spark 1.1 / 1.2 / 1.3$1.25$4.25$5.50MetaGLM-5.3$1.40$4.40$5.80Z.AIGrok 4.6 — <200K prompt tokens$2.00$6.00$8.00xAIMiMo-V2.5 Pro (>256K)$2.00$6.00$8.00XiaomiQwen3.8-Max$2.00$6.00$8.00QwenCloudGemini 3.7 Flash — starting Jan. 1, 2027$1.50$7.50$9.00GoogleGemini 3.8 Flash — starting Jan. 1, 2027$1.50$7.50$9.00GoogleGPT-5.6 Terra$2.00$12.00$14.00OpenAIGrok 4.6 — ≥200K prompt tokens$4.00$12.00$16.00xAIGPT-5.4$2.50$15.00$17.50OpenAIKimi K3$3.00$15.00$18.00Moonshot AIClaude Opus 5$5.00$25.00$30.00AnthropicSakana Fugu Ultra (≤272K)$5.00$30.00$35.00Sakana AIGPT-5.6 Sol — Standard mode$5.00$30.00$35.00OpenAIClaude Fable 5 / Claude Mythos 5$10.00$50.00$60.00AnthropicClaude Fable 5.1 / Claude Mythos 5.1$10.00$50.00$60.00AnthropicGPT-5.6 Sol — Fast mode$10.00$60.00$70.00OpenAIThat makes Zuckerberg’s “almost too cheap to meter” line less a statement about lower token prices than about what Meta believes developers can accomplish with those tokens.Artificial Analysis offers evidence for that argument, but also a complication. It measures Muse Spark 1.3 xhigh at 235.2 output tokens per second and estimates a cost of $0.55 per Intelligence Index task. At 61 on the Intelligence Index, that gives it the lowest cost per task of any currently measured model at that intelligence level. Muse Spark 1.2 cost only $0.40 per Artificial Analysis task, while scoring 57. Despite unchanged per-token pricing, the independent benchmark’s cost of completing an average task therefore increased generation-over-generation. Artificial Analysis attributes the increase primarily to heavier input-token consumption on agentic evaluations. That does not directly contradict Meta’s claim of 25% lower token use: Meta is describing comparisons in its own coding workflows, while Artificial Analysis is measuring a broader suite of reasoning and agentic tasks. But it illustrates why “cheap” becomes slippery once models operate as agents. Token rates, reasoning effort, number of turns, tool calls and retries all contribute to the actual cost of finishing work.Meta also retains its unusually cheap Contributor tier — $0.10 per million input tokens and $0.20 per million output tokens — in exchange for permission to use prompts and completions for training. As VentureBeat noted with Muse Spark 1.2, that may be attractive for prototyping but creates a materially different data-governance calculation for enterprises working with proprietary code or sensitive internal information.Wang’s ‘Gemini who?’ lands on an unusually close comparisonMeta chief AI officer Alexandr Wang was considerably less qualified in celebrating the release.After Artificial Analysis posted its Muse Spark results, Wang reposted them on X, adding: “i really hate to say it, but… gemini who? 😱💨”The shade was particularly pointed because Google released Gemini 3.8 Flash on the same day, pitching it at almost exactly the same class of workload: long-horizon software engineering, autonomous agents and multi-step professional reasoning. Google calls 3.8 its best reasoning and coding Flash model yet and says it is the company’s third Flash release in six weeks. Independent numbers give Wang something to work with, though hardly a knockout.Artificial Analysis gives Muse Spark 1.3 xhigh a 61 Intelligence Index score at $0.55 per task, compared with 59 and $0.58 for Gemini 3.8 Flash at high reasoning. Meta therefore edges Google on both intelligence and task cost at those particular settings. Google wins decisively on throughput. Artificial Analysis measures Gemini 3.8 Flash high at about 305 output tokens per second, versus 235 for Muse Spark — roughly 30% faster. Gemini also has the lower raw API sticker price for now: Google is charging an introductory $0.75 per million input tokens and $3.75 per million output tokens, compared with Meta’s $1.25 and $4.25.That promotional Google pricing expires December 31, after which it rises to $1.50 per million input tokens and $7.50 per million output tokens. The result is a useful snapshot of how tight frontier-model economics have become. Meta currently wins this independent comparison by two Intelligence Index points and three cents per benchmark task; Google offers substantially higher output throughput and cheaper raw tokens during its launch promotion.Wang’s “gemini who?” is fun executive trash talk. For an enterprise architect, the answer is closer to: Gemini is the faster option; Muse is currently the slightly stronger high-effort agent by this independent measure.Meta's evolving open weights stanceThe more consequential issue for some developers may have little to do with today’s benchmark race.When Meta launched Muse Code and Muse Spark 1.2 in August, VentureBeat noted how dramatically the company had moved away from the open-weight strategy that made Llama ubiquitous. Muse Code and Spark 1.2 were proprietary, API-served products — a striking posture for the company that had spent years arguing that open AI was the path forward.Five days later, Meta changed course again.On August 10, it released the 30-billion-parameter Muse Glimmer under an Apache 2.0 license. Zuckerberg also said: “In the coming weeks, we are also going to open the weights for Muse Spark 1.2.” Reuters separately reported Meta’s initiative to release the Spark 1.2 weights. Now, Meta has instead shipped Muse Spark 1.3 as another proprietary model.That does not yet amount to a broken promise — “coming weeks” can reasonably describe a period longer than three weeks. But today’s announcement makes the roadmap less clear rather than more.Meta’s upcoming post no longer says Muse Spark 1.2. It says its roadmap includes “the Muse Spark open weights release”, without identifying a version, release date, model size or license. Meta’s newest AI model Muse Spark 1.3, unveiled yesterday, is faster and more performant on third-party benchmarks than its predecessor — with a caveat.

"Muse Spark 1.3 is rolling out today with frontier performance almost too cheap to meter," Meta co-founder and CEO Mark Zuckerberg wrote on X, calling it Meta’s “biggest jump” yet in coding and agentic work.

Industry observers note that there is substance behind both parts of that claim. Muse Spark 1.3 makes significant gains over last month’s 1.2 release, particularly on long-running agent tasks. The version developers can access now is also one of the strongest price-performance offerings near the top of independent model rankings.

Meta’s strongest Muse Spark 1.3 benchmark results come from its max reasoning configuration. Meta says that version is still completing additional safety testing and will arrive “shortly”; the third-party benchmarking firm Artificial Analysis says it evaluated max in a limited partner preview, and currently lists no API provider at all for the configuration.

The version broadly rolling out this week through its Muse Code harness and the Meta Model API uses Meta’s previously available reasoning settings, including xhigh.

That makes the more relevant enterprise question not whether Muse Spark 1.3 can reach frontier territory, but how close the model companies can actually deploy today gets — and at what real cost.

Sources indicate that meta does disclose results for both configurations in its underlying evaluation report, so this is not a case of the tech giant hiding the deployable model. But its launch materials prominently showcase the max variant, and some of the largest scores belong to that configuration.

For example, Meta reports GDPval-AA v2 scores of 1,754 Elo for max versus 1,709 for xhigh, OSWorld 2.0 scores of 66.9 versus 57.2, and JobBench scores of 64.9 versus 61.2.

On some tests the distinction is negligible or reversed: DeepSearchQA is tied at 89.4, while xhigh scores 89.2 on Terminal-Bench 2.1 versus max at 88.8.

According to recent reports, artificial Analysis scores Muse Spark 1.3 max at 62 on its Intelligence Index and the shipping xhigh version at 61. The latter ties GPT-5.6 Sol max, Grok 4.6 high and Claude Opus 5 high. But Anthropic still occupies the top of the leaderboard: Claude Fable 5.1 reaches 66 at max and 65 at xhigh, while Claude Opus 5 reaches 63 at max and xhigh.

In other words, Muse Spark 1.3 xhigh is legitimately in the frontier cluster, but it is not the model currently setting the frontier.

That is still a substantial change from Muse Spark 1.2. VentureBeat’s coverage of last month’s launch found Meta fielding a credible coding challenger that nevertheless generally trailed Anthropic’s best model. Muse Spark 1.2 scored 82.9% on Terminal-Bench 2.1 versus Opus 5’s 86.7%, and also finished behind Opus on the other main coding comparisons Meta presented.

Recent findings suggest that with 1.3, Meta is no longer merely showing up in that contest. On several coding and agentic evaluations, it is trading wins with OpenAI and Anthropic.

Meta states the underlying model has also become easier to operate. Muse Spark 1.3 is trained to maintain multiple workflows in a long thread, gather context with tools, detect gaps in its own prepares, ask consumers for clarification when necessary and confirm before consequential actions. In Meta engineers’ internal comparisons, it used roughly 20% fewer tool calls and 25% fewer tokens than 1.2 during coding work.

For enterprises paying for thousands or millions of agent loops, those behavioral improvements could matter more than another leaderboard point.

Muse Spark 1.3 did not receive an API price cut. Meta kept Standard pricing exactly where it was for Muse Spark 1.2: $1.25 per million input tokens, $4.25 per million output tokens and $0.15 per million cached input tokens.

That makes Zuckerberg’s “almost too cheap to meter” line less a statement about lower token prices than about what Meta believes developers can accomplish with those tokens.

Sources indicate that artificial Analysis offers evidence for that argument, but also a complication. It measures Muse Spark 1.3 xhigh at 235.2 output tokens per second and estimates a cost of $0.55 per Intelligence Index task.

At 61 on the Intelligence Index, that gives it the lowest cost per task of any currently measured model at that intelligence level.

Muse Spark 1.2 cost only $0.40 per Artificial Analysis task, while scoring 57.

Sources indicate that despite unchanged per-token pricing, the independent benchmark’s cost of completing an average task therefore increased generation-over-generation. Artificial Analysis attributes the increase primarily to heavier input-token consumption on agentic evaluations.

That does not directly contradict Meta’s claim of 25% lower token use: Meta is describing comparisons in its own coding workflows, while Artificial Analysis is measuring a broader suite of reasoning and agentic tasks.

It has been revealed that but it illustrates why “cheap” becomes slippery once models operate as agents. Token rates, reasoning effort, number of turns, tool calls and retries all contribute to the actual cost of finishing work.

Meta also retains its unusually cheap Contributor tier — $0.10 per million input tokens and $0.20 per million output tokens — in exchange for permission to use prompts and completions for training.

As VentureBeat noted with Muse Spark 1.2, that may be attractive for prototyping but creates a materially different data-governance calculation for enterprises working with proprietary code or sensitive internal information.

Meta chief AI officer Alexandr Wang was considerably less qualified in celebrating the release.

Industry observers note that after Artificial Analysis posted its Muse Spark results, Wang reposted them on X, adding: “i really hate to say it, but… gemini who? 😱💨”.

Sources indicate that the shade was particularly pointed because Google released Gemini 3.8 Flash on the same day, pitching it at almost exactly the same class of workload: long-horizon software engineering, autonomous agents and multi-step professional reasoning. Google calls 3.8 its best reasoning and coding Flash model yet and indicates it is the organization’s third Flash release in six weeks.

Independent numbers give Wang something to work with, though hardly a knockout.

Artificial Analysis gives Muse Spark 1.3 xhigh a 61 Intelligence Index score at $0.55 per task, compared with 59 and $0.58 for Gemini 3.8 Flash at high reasoning. Meta therefore edges Google on both intelligence and task cost at those particular settings.

Google wins decisively on throughput. Artificial Analysis measures Gemini 3.8 Flash high at about 305 output tokens per second, versus 235 for Muse Spark — roughly 30% faster. Gemini also has the lower raw API sticker price for now: Google is charging an introductory $0.75 per million input tokens and $3.75 per million output tokens, compared with Meta’s $1.25 and $4.25.

That promotional Google pricing expires December 31, after which it rises to $1.50 per million input tokens and $7.50 per million output tokens.

Industry observers note that the result is a useful snapshot of how tight frontier-model economics have become. Meta right now wins this independent comparison by two Intelligence Index points and three cents per benchmark task; Google offers substantially higher output throughput and cheaper raw tokens during its launch promotion.

Wang’s “gemini who?” is fun executive trash talk. For an enterprise architect, the answer is closer to: Gemini is the faster option; Muse is at the moment the slightly stronger high-effort agent by this independent measure.

The more consequential problem for some developers may have little to do with today’s benchmark race.

When Meta released Muse Code and Muse Spark 1.2 in August, VentureBeat noted how dramatically the company had moved away from the open-weight strategy that made Llama ubiquitous.

Muse Code and Spark 1.2 were proprietary, API-served products — a striking posture for the company that had spent years arguing that open AI was the path forward.

Five days later, Meta changed course again.

On August 10, it released the 30-billion-parameter Muse Glimmer under an Apache 2.0 license. Zuckerberg also noted: “In the coming weeks, we are also going to open the weights for Muse Spark 1.2.” Reuters separately reported Meta’s strategy to release the Spark 1.2 weights.

Now, Meta has instead shipped Muse Spark 1.3 as another proprietary model.

That does not yet amount to a broken promise — “coming weeks” can reasonably describe a period longer than three weeks. But today’s announcement makes the roadmap less clear rather than more.

It has been revealed that meta’s new post no longer indicates Muse Spark 1.2. It says its roadmap includes “the Muse Spark open weights release”, without identifying a version, release date, model size or license. Zuckerberg likewise remarked on X that “Muse Spark open weights releases” are coming soon.

For teams that standardized on Llama because downloadable weights meant self-hosting, customization and control over inference economics, that ambiguity may matter more than whether Spark gained another point on a composite benchmark.

Industry observers note that muse Spark 1.3 shows that Meta can now iterate proprietary frontier models at extraordinary speed. The shipping xhigh configuration is fast, competitively priced and much closer to the top of independent rankings than its predecessors. The max preview shows Meta can push the family a little further when allowed to spend more reasoning compute.

The next test is different: whether Meta can convert that pace into a roadmap enterprises can actually strategy around — including making its best capabilities broadly deployable and delivering the open-weight Spark model it has already noted is coming.
